🧠 Crypto News Brief: Crypto spent the weekend digesting the largest theft in its history: the FBI named North Korea, Binance reopened withdrawals and Bitcoin steadied near $78K. Fresh breaches and Beijing's crackdown kept sentiment cautious. 🕵️ FBI Blames North Korea for $6B Binance Heist The FBI said on Saturday that North Korea's TraderTraitor hacking unit was behind the theft of more than $6 billion from Binance, the largest crypto heist on record. Working with the Secret Service and IRS-CI, the bureau says the attackers are swapping the loot mainly into ether and are expected to launder it through DeFi and instant-swap services. Read full story 🔓 Binance Reopens Withdrawals, Covers 95% of Losses Binance began restoring withdrawals on Sunday, starting with bitcoin and adding ether, USDT, USDC, BNB and XRP across 15 other blockchains, with remaining assets returning only after security checks. The exchange now says it has covered about 95% of the stolen amount, up from 90%, and insists users will not absorb the loss. More details 📈 Bitcoin Steadies Near $78K After Hack Sell-Off Bitcoin climbed back toward $78,000 on Sunday, recovering from the Binance-driven sell-off that dragged it to a six-week low near $76,100. Major coins traded in a narrow weekend range, while Lighter (LIT) led the altcoin pack with a gain of roughly 18%. Read more 🇨🇳 China's Communist Party Targets Crypto Bribery A Central Committee resolution published by Xinhua on November 1 calls for a tougher fight against corruption carried out through virtual currencies, blockchain and cross-border capital flows. Investigators are told to pursue officials who use digital assets to take bribes or hide illicit wealth, while China's existing crypto trading restrictions stay in force. See details 🤖 AI-Assisted Hacker Breaches Chainalysis Blockchain analytics firm Chainalysis disclosed that an attacker using AI-driven agentic techniques broke into its systems and internal tools this month, accessing customer names, emails, user IDs and role labels. The company says credentials, session tokens and investigation data were not touched, and that the incident is unrelated to the Binance theft. Does it really matter which rice you eat?



Sam Wikeley

Science correspondent



 Occasionally, when standing in the supermarket aisle, my hand will hover over a bag of brown rice. Conventional wisdom suggests it is healthier than its white counterpart and, indeed, it does contain more fibre, magnesium and other wholesome nutrients. Personal experience, however, suggests it is far less delicious. Shamefully, that latter consideration usually outweighs the former, and I grab a bag of white rice instead.

81751.subject: Britain’s boring Budget
81751.body:
Editor's Digest 

Автор: Financial Times


Автор: Financial Times

    
    
    Прочитайте цю статтю на LinkedIn, щоб приєднатися до обговорення
Прочитати на LinkedIn
https://www.linkedin.com/comm/pulse/britains-boring-budget-financial-times-y0bbe?lipi=urn%3Ali%3Apage%3Aemail_email_series_follow_newsletter_02%3BWRwifjVRQe2YZTWrqvdolg%3D%3D&midToken=AQFTjFOONAfT2w&midSig=1SeXHB6Si07Iw1&trk=eml-email_series_follow_newsletter_02-null-0-read_more_banner_cta_&trkEmail=eml-email_series_follow_newsletter_02-null-0-read_more_banner_cta_-null-fz96fz~mvw4yds8~xj-null-null&eid=fz96fz-mvw4yds8-xj
  
Welcome to your Editor’s Choice on what has been one of the busiest weeks of the year, with three elections in Brazil, Serbia and Israel, and, most importantly, the unveiling of the UK Budget. Readers outside the UK may be baffled by the spectacle that is our Budget, a perfectly choreographed show that has the whole nation holding its breath. The newsroom is buzzing on Budget day, with reporters and editors huddled around the main news desk to listen to the chancellor deliver his speech, and then to our economics editor share his main takeaways. It is also the only day of the year when we publish two newspapers in the UK, including a full print Budget supplement with its own front page.  So what about the Budget? It was, as we wrote in our FT View, a Budget designed to buy time and delay the hard decisions. Instead of a decisive plan to cut the welfare bill, boost defence spending and spur growth, chancellor John Healey made only modest commitments on tax and spending, including a £100 handout to help households with winter energy bills. Our crack team of reporters and columnists answer the big questions about the Budget on Political Fix. For more on what the Budget means for your money, read our full breakdown here. And with inflation on the up and tax thresholds still frozen, use our new fiscal drag calculator to find out how much more tax you could be paying in the years ahead. My choices this week We finally got our hands on Anthropic’s IPO prospectus on Monday. And it didn’t disappoint. From $800bn in data centre commitments to an extraordinary governance structure, we learnt a lot from the 240,000-word document. But as our tech writer Richard Waters points out, it’s what isn’t in the listing that points to some of the biggest questions about Anthropic’s business and the wider AI sector. Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva made a stunning comeback in Brazil’s presidential election run-off last Sunday, beating rival Flávio Bolsonaro (who subsequently fled to the US). Lula’s victory is surely his greatest political triumph. But his re-election has also triggered a powerful market rout. Eighty-one-year-old Lula has a fiscal reckoning on his hands. Israel’s election delivered a far less decisive outcome than those in Brazil and Serbia (where Aleksandar Vučić was ousted after 12 years in charge). Neither Benjamin Netanyahu’s far-right coalition nor the opposi
